newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST- GOOD SALES TO DRIVE TOYOTA YR SHR.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- GOOD SALES TO DRIVE TOYOTA YR SHR.

text.p: Toyota South Africa Ltd would post a rise in earnings for the year ending December 31, 1996 boosted by its good grip on vehicle sales, analysts said on Thursday.
They said the results could even surprise with better results than anticipated and would continue its grip on vehicle sales despite an expected slowdown in sales this year.

"There may be a surprise in the result...Toyota is doing quite well with sales. It is a strong player. Sales (overall) may go down for 1997/98 but Toyota is doing better than the market," an industry analyst who declined to be identified said.

Analysts polled by Reuters forecast earnings per share rising to between 490 and 530 cents with consensus at 515 cents -- an improvement of 7.92 percent from 477.2 reported for the year ending December 31, 1995.
They expected a dividend range of 83 to 90 cents, with consensus at 86.6 cents compared with the previous year's 80 cents, equal to an increase of 8.25 percent.
South African new car sales rose 5.62 percent to 249,884 units in 1996 compared to 236,584 in 1995. Toyota topped individual manufatures sales for most months in 1996.
In January this year, Toyota led the field with sales of 6,483, with its nearest rival Volkswagen netting 5,462 sales.
Analysts said its share price lagged behind its earnings potential.
"It is extremely undervalued. The share price doesn't reflect the quality of the company it is," SMK's Franca di Silvestro said.
"I think they are going to have a better share than people expect them to," she added.

Toyota Motor Corp's relationship with the South African manufacturer, following its purchase of a 28 percent stake valued at 446 million rand last October, was a positive factor boosting confidence in the company, analysts said.
Toyota South Africa chairman Bert Wessels said at the time of the announcement the deal would help the company accelerate its production technology to world standards.

A 15-day strike by Toyota workers in KwaZulu-Natal last March, which dented vehicle output by 6,450 vehicles and saw workers losing 1.2 million rand a day, would not have a major impact on the results, analysts said.
